scenes.visual: Title card: Conservation and Restoration. Main title: Protect Habitat, Support Recovery.

scenes.tts: Conservation starts with what drove a population down. If habitat loss is the cause, address it first. Protect habitat, connect isolated patches, and help damaged ecosystems recover. Small populations can also need extra help with chance and inbreeding. A genetic gain may be temporary if habitat keeps shrinking.

scenes.visual: Show habitat shrinking around a wild cat population. Halt the loss, protect a patch, connect patches and show damaged habitat recovering. Keep a small isolated population visible as the reason additional measures may be needed.

scenes.tts: What does the evidence show? In a randomized experiment at one South Carolina site, connected patches of equal area gained plant species faster and lost them more slowly. That does not establish how corridors work everywhere. Across conservation trials, action improved biodiversity or slowed its decline in about two thirds of cases compared with no action. Recovery can still be incomplete. Active restoration did not, on average, outperform ending the disturbance, though few studies compared them directly.

scenes.visual: Show equal-area connected and unconnected habitat treatments, with a label identifying the randomized South Carolina experiment. Animate faster species gains and slower losses in connected patches. Then clearly switch to a separate conservation-wide synthesis: action versus no action, with about two-thirds showing improvement or slower decline. Finally compare active restoration with ending disturbance; show incomplete recovery and label the limited direct comparisons. Do not depict the two-thirds result as restoration-only.

scenes.tts: Why give small populations extra help? Chance in who survives and breeds matters more when numbers are low. Drift erodes genetic variation. Inbreeding lowers survival and fertility. Fewer animals mean more inbreeding, which can mean fewer animals again.

scenes.visual: Show a small population losing individuals through chance, then genetic variation fading. Draw the feedback loop: fewer animals, more inbreeding, lower survival, fewer animals. Do not reuse the five-offspring probability calculation.

scenes.tts: The head count also misses something. Effective size is the size of an idealised population that would lose genetic variation at the same rate. Unequal offspring numbers, uneven sex ratios and population swings usually make it smaller than the count.

scenes.visual: Contrast census size N with effective size Ne. Show unequal offspring contributions, uneven breeding sex ratios and population swings, then a smaller effective-size bar. Remove the sex-ratio formula and target conversion.

scenes.tts: Genetic rescue can improve fitness by bringing in animals from another population. After eight Texas females were released into Florida, panther numbers about tripled and heterozygosity doubled. But managers must weigh disease and whether donors suit local conditions. Monitor survival, reproduction and genetics. A later study found the population stabilised and declined from twenty sixteen to twenty twenty.

Show population and heterozygosity increasing, alongside monitoring of survival, reproduction and genetics. End with the 2016 to 2020 stabilisation and decline; show donor suitability and disease as risks to assess.

scenes.tts: Population viability analysis helps compare management options. Run a population model many times. The fraction that goes extinct within a chosen time estimates the risk. A minimum viable population is the smallest isolated population meeting a chosen persistence target in a given habitat. Read model results with their assumptions and uncertainty. Even the ranking of options can change with model structure.

scenes.visual: Show repeated simulated population trajectories under alternative management scenarios. Label extinction risk as extinct runs divided by total runs within the chosen horizon, without invented numerical outputs. Display chosen persistence target, time and habitat beside minimum viable population. Change model structure to show that option rankings can change.

scenes.tts: Evidence says what an option is likely to do. It does not choose which outcome matters most. Set out biological, social and economic goals with the people affected, then compare the tradeoffs.
